notation.title: Infix, postfix and prefix

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: An operand is a value, such as A or B.
An operator is an action, such as +.
Infix, prefix and postfix describe where the operator is written.

sections.title: Three ways to write an expression
bullets: The operands stay in their logical order.
The position of the operator changes.

sections.title: How to read the example
bullets: First calculate A+B. Then multiply the result by C.
In postfix, AB+ forms the sum; C* multiplies it. In prefix, the first * combines +AB with C.
For A+B*C, multiplication happens first: postfix ABC*+ and prefix +A*BC.
Infix needs precedence and sometimes parentheses. Unambiguous prefix/postfix expressions do not need parentheses. A stack can evaluate them.

queue-array.title: Queue and sequential representation

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A queue follows “first in, first out”, like people waiting at a counter.
Insert at the rear and remove from the front.
An array can store these items.

sections.title: Queue
bullets: A queue follows FIFO: the first item inserted is the first removed.
Enqueue inserts at the rear; dequeue removes from the front.

sections.title: Array representation
bullets: Store elements in consecutive array positions Q[0..N-1]. At the start front=0 and rear=-1; the queue is empty when front>rear.

sections.title: Operations
sections.code:
ENQUEUE(x):
  if rear == N-1: report full
  else: rear = rear+1; Q[rear] = x
DEQUEUE():
  if front > rear: report empty
  else: x = Q[front]; front = front+1; return x

sections.title: Example and limitation
bullets: Enqueue 10,20,30 gives front=0 and rear=2. Dequeue returns 10 and moves front to 1.
Both operations take O(1).
In this simple linear representation, free positions before front cannot be reused after rear reaches N-1. A circular queue reuses them.
Printing and service-request scheduling are FIFO applications.

linked.title: Sequential storage and linked lists

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: An array keeps items next to one another in memory. A linked list keeps items in nodes, with each node storing a link to the next node.

sections.title: Drawbacks of sequential storage
bullets: An array uses a next to one another memory block and has a fixed capacity after allocation.
Inserting or deleting in the middle shifts later elements: O(n) time.
An oversized array wastes reserved space; growing it may need allocation and copying.

sections.title: Linked-list representation
bullets: Each node stores data and a pointer to the next node.
Nodes need not occupy adjacent memory addresses. head points to the first node; NULL ends a singly linked list.

sections.title: Example and trade-offs
bullets: To insert 15 after node 10: new->next = node10->next, then node10->next = new. Only links change.
Insertion/deletion is O(1) when the required predecessor is already known.
Finding it takes O(n).
Linked lists grow node by node, but need pointer memory, have no O(1) index access, and often have poorer cache locality than arrays.

reverse-print.title: Recursive linked-list output

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A recursive function first visits the next node and prints the current node while returning.
This can print values in reverse order without reversing the links.

sections.title: Correct option
bullets: B — prints all nodes in reverse order.
It does not reverse the links.

sections.title: Why
bullets: The NULL check stops recursion. Each call first processes head->next and prints its own data only after that call returns. So the last node prints first.

sections.title: Cost
bullets: Output: 30 20 10.
Time O(n); recursion stack O(n).
An empty list prints nothing.

circular-push.title: Circular list and stack push

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: In a circular list, the last node points back to the first. A stack inserts and removes at its top.
Follow the pointer updates in the stated order.

sections.title: Circular list
bullets: The last node points to the first node instead of NULL. A stack must insert and remove from the same logical end to provide LIFO.

sections.title: Pointer convention
bullets: Use stack as a tail pointer. The top node is stack->next. This makes push O(1). An empty stack is NULL; a one-node stack points to itself. This convention is chosen explicitly because the question does not specify it.

sections.title: C function
Effect
bullets: For top 10 → 20 → tail 30, push(5) creates top 5 → 10 → 20 → 30 → 5. The tail remains 30. Call push(&stack,5). Allocation failure leaves the old list unchanged.

stack.title: Stack as an ADT

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A stack follows “last in, first out”, like a stack of plates.
Push adds an item to the top; pop removes the top item.

sections.title: Meaning
bullets: A stack is an abstract data type with LIFO order: the last item pushed is the first popped.
The ADT specifies behaviour independently of array or linked-list storage.

sections.title: Abstract interface
sections.code:
abstract typedef <<eltype>> Stack;
create() -> empty Stack
push(S, x: eltype) -> insert x at top
pop(S) -> remove and return top element
peek(S) -> return top without removing
isEmpty(S) -> boolean
/* pop/peek require a non-empty stack. */

sections.title: Array implementation
bullets: Use an array A[N] and top=-1 at the start. Push: check top<N-1, then A[++top]=x. Pop: check top>=0, then return A[top--]. A full array causes overflow; popping an empty stack causes underflow.

sections.title: Example and uses
bullets: push(10), push(20), push(30) makes 30 the top. pop() returns 30; the next pop returns 20.
Push, pop and peek take O(1).
Applications include function calls, undo history, parenthesis matching and expression evaluation.

list-edit.title: Insert and remove linked-list nodes

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: To insert or remove a linked-list node, change the links that connect it to nearby nodes.
Handle an empty list and the first node separately.

sections.title: Representation
bullets: Use head for the first node and NULL for the end.
The examples use a singly linked list.
Always check allocation and empty-list cases.

sections.title: Insert a node
bullets: At the beginning: new->next=head; head=new.
After a known node p: new->next=p->next; p->next=new.
At the end: set new->next=NULL; if empty, head=new; otherwise find the last node and set last->next=new.

sections.title: Remove a node
bullets: At the beginning: if non-empty, save old=head; head=head->next; free(old).
After predecessor p: save old=p->next; if old exists, p->next=old->next; free(old).
At the end: if empty do nothing; if one node free it and set head=NULL; otherwise find the penultimate node, free its next node, then set its next=NULL.

sections.title: Example and cost
bullets: 10 → 20 → 30; insert 15 after 10 → 10 → 15 → 20 → 30. Remove 20 by linking 15 directly to 30 before freeing 20.
Beginning operations are O(1).
Given a predecessor, link changes are O(1); searching for a position or the end takes O(n) without extra pointers.

doubly.title: Doubly linked list and applications

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A doubly linked list stores two links in each node: one to the previous node and one to the next.
This allows movement in both directions.

sections.title: Node structure
bullets: A node stores data, prev and next. head->prev=NULL and tail->next=NULL. Unlike a singly linked list, it can be traversed in both directions.

sections.title: Link updates
bullets: To insert new after p: new->prev=p; new->next=p->next; if p->next exists set p->next->prev=new; then p->next=new. Update tail if inserting after the old tail.
To delete known node x: reconnect x->prev to x->next and x->next to x->prev. Update head/tail at boundaries, then free(x).

sections.title: Compared with a singly linked list
Applications and limitation
bullets: Browser back/forward navigation, undo/redo lists, music playlists and LRU cache ordering need movement or removal in both directions.
Extra pointer memory and more link updates are the cost.
Searching for a value still takes O(n).

bullets: A data structure is a way to organize data so that it can be stored and used efficiently.
Choose it according to the operations you need.

sections.title: Definition
bullets: A data structure is a way of organising and storing data so that operations such as access, search, insertion and deletion can be performed efficiently.

bullets: Static capacity: an array has a fixed number of slots after allocation.

Homogeneous: elements share one type, such as an integer array. Heterogeneous: a record/struct contains fields of different types.

bullets: Use arrays for fast indexed access, stacks for LIFO, queues for FIFO, trees for hierarchies and graphs for networks.

btree.title: B-tree of order n

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A B-tree is a balanced search tree that stores several keys in one node.
Its leaves stay at the same level, helping searches remain short.

sections.title: Definition and convention
bullets: A B-tree is a balanced multiway search tree.
Here order n means at most n children and n−1 keys per node.
Some books instead use a minimum degree t; do not mix the two conventions.

sections.title: Properties
bullets: Keys within a node are sorted; child subtrees separate the key ranges.
A non-root node has at least ceil(n/2) children if internal, and at least ceil(n/2)−1 keys.
A non-empty root has at least one key. An internal root has at least two children.
All leaves are at the same depth.

sections.title: Insertion
bullets: Find the appropriate leaf and insert in sorted order.
If a node exceeds its allowed keys, split it and promote a separator to its parent; repeat upwards if needed.
Splitting the root increases the height.
The following order-4 example uses splitting full nodes before descent.

sections.title: Final tree and use
bullets: Root [10,20] routes values <10 to the left, between 10 and 20 to the middle, and >20 to the right.
Search and insertion need O(log m) levels for m stored keys.
B-trees reduce disk accesses in database and file indexes.

matrix.title: Adjacency matrix: forms and applications

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: An adjacency matrix is a table showing which graph vertices are connected.
Row i and column j record the connection from vertex i to vertex j.

sections.title: Representation
bullets: For n vertices, an adjacency matrix is an n×n table.
Row i and column j describe the edge from i to j.
Fix the vertex order before filling it.

sections.title: Other forms
bullets: Directed, unweighted: A[i][j]=1 only when i→j exists. The matrix need not be symmetric.
Undirected: A[i][j]=A[j][i], so the matrix is symmetric.
Weighted: store the edge weight. Represent a missing edge by a separate flag or ∞, since 0 can be a valid weight. For shortest-path initialization, set the diagonal to 0.
A diagonal entry may represent a self-loop in an adjacency matrix. For a simple unweighted graph it is 0.

sections.title: Costs and applications
bullets: Space O(n²); test an edge in O(1); list all neighbours of one vertex in O(n).
It suits dense graphs, small fixed networks and matrix-based algorithms such as Floyd–Warshall.
Sparse graphs usually use adjacency lists to save space.

traversals.title: Binary-tree traversal methods

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Tree traversal means visiting every node in a chosen order.
Preorder, inorder and postorder differ in when they visit the root.

sections.title: Meaning
bullets: Traversal visits each node systematically.
Use the same tree for all four orders below.

rows: A B D E C F
D B E A C F
D E B F C A
A B C D E F

sections.title: Recursive pattern
sections.code:
TRAVERSE(node):
  if node == NULL: return
  visit(node)       // put here for preorder
  TRAVERSE(node.left)
  visit(node)       // OR here for inorder
  TRAVERSE(node.right)
  visit(node)       // OR here for postorder
// Use only ONE of the three visit positions.

sections.title: Cost and uses
bullets: Each traversal takes O(n).
Recursive traversals use O(h) stack space for height h; level order needs a queue up to the tree width.
Preorder copies a tree, inorder lists BST keys in sorted order, and postorder deletes a tree or evaluates an expression tree.

tree-ops.title: Binary-tree operations and applications

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Tree operations include adding, searching for and removing nodes.
The exact method depends on the type of tree.

sections.title: Basic operations
bullets: Create nodes with data, left and right pointers; initialise missing children to NULL.
Traverse using preorder, inorder, postorder or level order.
Search a general binary tree by traversal: O(n) in the worst case.
Insert or delete according to the tree’s purpose; an arbitrary binary tree has no automatic ordering rule.

sections.title: If the tree is a binary search tree
bullets: For distinct keys, left subtree keys are smaller and right subtree keys are larger.
Insert by following comparisons to a vacant child.
Delete a leaf directly; replace a one-child node by its child; for two children, replace its key by its inorder successor and delete that successor.

These rules apply to a BST, not every binary tree.

sections.title: Applications
bullets: Expression trees organise operators and operands; binary search trees support ordered dictionaries; binary heaps implement priority queues; decision trees represent yes/no choices.

graph-complex.title: Graphs and three traversal difficulties

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Graph traversal visits vertices through their edges.
Unlike a tree, a graph may contain cycles, several paths to one vertex or separate components.

sections.title: Graph
bullets: G=(V,E) has a set of vertices and edges. The illustrated graph has four vertices and four undirected edges.

sections.title: Three reasons traversal is more involved
bullets: Cycles: following links can return to an already visited vertex and loop forever without a visited set.
Multiple paths: the same vertex may be reached through different neighbours; mark it visited before exploring further to avoid duplicate processing.
Disconnected components and no natural root: one starting vertex may not reach the whole graph. Choose a start and run traversal again from each remaining unvisited vertex.

sections.title: How to handle this
bullets: DFS uses recursion/a stack; BFS uses a queue.
Both maintain visited flags. A tree has a unique path between vertices and a rooted tree offers a natural start; a simple linked list follows one next link at each step.

dfs.title: Depth-first traversal

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Depth-first search (DFS) follows one path as far as possible, then returns to try another path.
Mark visited vertices to avoid repeating them.

sections.title: Idea
bullets: DFS explores one path as deeply as possible, then backtracks to the most recent vertex with an unvisited neighbour.
Use recursion or an explicit stack.

sections.title: Algorithm
Worked example
bullets: For the pictured graph, start at A and choose neighbours alphabetically. Visit A → B → D → C. At C, A and D are already visited; backtrack until finished. Another neighbour order can produce a different valid DFS order.

sections.title: Cost and applications
bullets: With adjacency lists: O(V+E) time and O(V) extra memory.
With a matrix: O(V²) time.
Applications include connected components, path existence, cycle detection and topological sorting of a DAG.
Cycle detection needs parent tracking for undirected graphs or active-recursion states for directed graphs.

circular.title: Circular linked list

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A circular linked list has no null link at its end: the last node points back to the first.
Stop a traversal when you return to the starting node.

sections.title: Structure
bullets: A circular linked list links its last node back to the first.
An empty list can be represented by NULL; a one-node list points to itself.

sections.title: Traversal
Example and operations
bullets: 10 → 20 → 30 → 10 repeats in a circle. Stop after returning to head, not at NULL.
With a tail pointer, head=tail->next. To append a new node: new->next=tail->next; tail->next=new; tail=new. For an empty list, set new->next=new and tail=new.

sections.title: Uses and cost
bullets: Round-robin scheduling and circular queues repeatedly cycle through items.
Traversal takes O(n); insertion after a known node takes O(1).
Broken links or an incorrect stopping condition can cause an infinite loop.

end-edit.title: Insertion and deletion at the end

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: To add at the end, connect the last node to the new node.
To delete the last node, find its predecessor and change that predecessor’s link.

sections.title: Assumption
bullets: A singly linked list has head and no stored tail pointer.
Handle an empty list and a one-node list separately.

sections.title: Insert at end
sections.code:
INSERT_END(head, x):
  new = allocate node; if failed: return head
  new.data = x; new.next = NULL
  if head == NULL: return new
  p = head
  while p.next != NULL: p = p.next
  p.next = new
  return head

sections.title: Delete at end
sections.code:
DELETE_END(head):
  if head == NULL: return NULL
  if head.next == NULL:
    free(head); return NULL
  p = head
  while p.next.next != NULL: p = p.next
  free(p.next); p.next = NULL
  return head

sections.title: Example and complexity
bullets: Insert 40 into 10 → 20 → 30 to find 10 → 20 → 30 → 40; deleting the end restores 10 → 20 → 30. Both operations take O(n) with head only and O(1) extra space. A tail pointer speeds insertion, but deleting the tail still needs its predecessor in a singly linked list.

queue-adt.title: Queue ADT and implementation

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: A queue ADT describes what a queue does, without fixing how it is stored.
Its main operations are enqueue, dequeue and checking whether it is empty.

sections.title: Interface
bullets: A queue is FIFO.
Its operations are create, enqueue, dequeue, front/peek and isEmpty; a bounded implementation also offers isFull.
Enqueue adds at the rear and dequeue removes the oldest item.

sections.title: Circular-array implementation
sections.code:
State: Q[N], front=0, rear=0, count=0; N>0
ENQUEUE(x):
  if count == N: report overflow; return
  Q[rear] = x
  rear = (rear+1) mod N
  count = count+1
DEQUEUE():
  if count == 0: report underflow
  else:
    x = Q[front]
    front = (front+1) mod N
    count = count-1
    return x
PEEK(): require count>0; return Q[front]

sections.title: Example
bullets: For N=3, enqueue 10,20,30: count=3. Dequeue returns 10; enqueue 40 reuses index 0. Logical order is 20,30,40. The count distinguishes empty from full even when front==rear.

sections.title: Cost and applications
bullets: Enqueue/dequeue/peek take O(1), storage O(N).
The circular layout avoids wasted freed positions.
Uses include printer jobs, buffers and BFS.

merge.title: Merge sort

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Merge sort splits a list into smaller parts, sorts those parts and combines them in order.
The combining step is called merging.

sections.title: Principle
bullets: Divide the array into halves, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves.
Stop when a subarray has at most one element.

sections.title: Algorithm
sections.code:
MERGESORT(A):
  if length(A) <= 1: return A
  mid = floor(length(A)/2)
  L = MERGESORT(A[0:mid])
  R = MERGESORT(A[mid:])
  result = empty; i = j = 0
  while i < length(L) and j < length(R):
    if L[i] <= R[j]: append L[i] to result; i = i+1
    else: append R[j] to result; j = j+1
  append remaining L and remaining R
  return result

sections.title: Complexity and properties
bullets: At each level, merging processes n elements; there are O(log n) levels.
Time is O(n log n) in best, average and worst cases.
Standard array merge sort needs O(n) auxiliary storage plus O(log n) recursion stack.
It is stable when equal values are taken from the left half first.

merge.text:
Merge sort
Understand the idea
Merge sort splits a list into smaller parts, sorts those parts and combines them in order.
The combining step is called merging.


Principle
Divide the array into halves, sort each half recursively, then merge the two sorted halves.
Stop when a subarray has at most one element.


Algorithm
MERGESORT(A):
  if length(A) <= 1: return A
  mid = floor(length(A)/2)
  L = MERGESORT(A[0:mid])
  R = MERGESORT(A[mid:])
  result = empty; i = j = 0
  while i < length(L) and j < length(R):
    if L[i] <= R[j]: append L[i] to result; i = i+1
    else: append R[j] to result; j = j+1
  append remaining L and remaining R
  return result

search.title: Searching techniques and binary search

sections.title: Understand the idea
bullets: Searching finds a required value.
Linear search checks items one by one.
Binary search repeatedly halves the search range in sorted data.

sections.title: Binary-search algorithm
sections.code:
BINARY_SEARCH(A, x):
  low = 0; high = length(A)-1
  while low <= high:
    mid = low + floor((high-low)/2)
    if A[mid] == x: return mid
    if A[mid] < x: low = mid+1
    else: high = mid-1
  return NOT_FOUND

sections.title: Why it works and cost
bullets: Each comparison discards the half that cannot contain the target because the data is sorted.
Iterative binary search takes O(log n) time and O(1) extra space.
Sorting first has a separate cost; binary search should not be applied directly to an unsorted array.
